# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)

Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26.

## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)

Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:

- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.

Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).

---

## Philosophy and decision principles

- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]

- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]

- Force plates (CMJ testing) were already the department's longitudinal performance-tracking tool well before the 2022-23 wellness-survey experiment, and remained in place after that experiment ended. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg) — each with a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol. **Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)** [revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- Metric selection for force-plate reporting follows a disciplined framework: pick 1-2 output metrics (the obvious performance result, e.g. jump height), 1-3 driver metrics (what produces the output, e.g. braking/propulsive force), 1-3 strategy metrics (how the athlete achieved it, e.g. phase durations), optional symmetry metrics (L/R differences), and add "fluffy" metrics (peak power, average power, RFD) only with a specific, defensible rationale. **Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own** [hd-odsf-metrics.md — origin: Hawkin Dynamics]
- NordBord hamstring testing was retired for roster-wide football monitoring (after starting January 2023) because a 25-30 minute per-group session could not be sustained across 120+ athletes without large, uncontrolled gaps in the data, and staff turnover ended the coordination needed to run it at scale. The decision rule stated: keep a demanding test only where you have "smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose, dedicated oversight" (now used for targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing); drop it where you can't guarantee consistent, comparable collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

## Speed and sprint

- Linear sprint testing uses a 2-point start for team-sport athletes (for reliability), athlete self-selected start timing, at least two maximal-effort reps over 30-40 meters. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- SmartSpeed timing gates are the standard tool for sprint, agility, and reaction-time testing across the department. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity) and is described as harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power, but as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11]

- The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Inferred (transcript + shared course material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]

- The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34]
- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21]

- Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15]

## Conditioning and energy systems

- Conditioning is defined two ways: (1) how well an athlete can meet the energy requirements of their specific sport/activity, and (2) how well they sustain strength, speed, and power output across a full competition. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.22]
- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]
- Anaerobic (lactate) threshold heart-rate zones are assigned by athlete body size rather than a single number: roughly 165 bpm for big/tall athletes, 170 for medium, 175 for small, with Zone 1-4 bands set as percentages of that individual threshold. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.28-29]
- The traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest — this ordering is used to sequence what needs the most frequent re-exposure. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.47]
- Training intensities between roughly 75-90% of maximal effort are labeled (via Francis) "no man's land" — too fast to build alactic power cleanly, too slow to build real aerobic capacity — and are treated as a zone to generally avoid as a primary training target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.48]
- "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
- For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
- Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
- Joel Jamieson's *Ultimate MMA Conditioning* is recommended as the single best practical resource for energy-system development, on the basis that its methods transfer cleanly to non-combat sports despite the MMA framing. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md pp.49-50; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]

## Periodization and programming

- Macro/meso/microcycle structure is used as the standard planning language, with an explicit reminder that a "training week" does not have to equal 7 calendar days — it can be extended to fit training themes around a real competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.17-18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
- The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume), before a transition into competition. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]
- In-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity even when the practice schedule looks repetitive week to week, specifically to avoid training monotony for the athlete. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21]
- Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block — "you can't ride two horses with one saddle." Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29; week1-lecture.md p.70]
- An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract: lay out the competition calendar, key non-training dates (holidays, exam weeks), and phase-by-phase volume/intensity waves, then adapt the route as circumstances change while still reaching the same destination. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.22-23; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.13-15]
- Training residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue readiness for max-velocity work degrades. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
- The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.16]

None. Every one of the sixteen required sections had at least some material. Several sections are thin, though, and should be read as gaps rather than settled positions: **Rehab and return to play**, **Injury risk and prevention**, **Recovery and sleep**, **Nutrition and body composition**, and **Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach**. See `interview-prep.md`.

---

## Tensions and contradictions

1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.

2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.

3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.

4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.

5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.

6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]

7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.

8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.

9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.

10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.

# Case Study: An Elite Sprinter and a Hurdler on Run-Specific Isometrics

**What it is** — Natera presents two athletes (~93:07–101:49).

**Elite male sprinter.** He was a strong, "power-hungry" athlete: a good accelerator but poorly elastic, with a weak max velocity.
- **Baseline:** back squat about **2.65× BW**; isometric mid-thigh pull **5.78× BW**. It is unclear whether that was single- or double-leg; the pull came before Natera moved to iso squats. CMJ about **59–62 cm**.
- **GPP:** eccentric calf work, then hip ISO holds progressing to switches.
- **SPP:** ankle and hip ISO catches, plus "ISO stadium descents," a loaded, cyclical isometric step-down that comes after the continuum.
- **Loads cited:** ankle ISO catch "up to 160 kg" (the transcript says "leaving up to 160 kilo"), which is implausible against his own 60 kg example and needs verifying on video. Hip ISO catch about 35 kg.
- **Reported changes:** CMJ +3 cm; CMJ power (~6,000 W) +200–300 W; takeoff velocity up; **RSI** "improved significantly," which he calls the main win; shorter contact times at about 30–40 m; longer acceleration and higher max velocity (around 11 m/s).

**Female 100 m hurdler.** She was coached by a Polish coach whose name the ASR renders "Peter Marazu ski" (name unverified), with Natera collaborating. Her times stagnated in 2016–2017. Run-specific isometrics (RSI) were added in 2018 through mid-2019 alongside "track training" and traditional squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts. She used **holds and pushes only**, and progressed past targets such as a **2× BW ankle hold**. Afterwards her hurdle times and speed improved to "elite level." Her quote to a reporter: "I don't lift heavy weights. I just hold them."

*(Every number is single-source ASR from slides; the before/after charts are visual only. Verify at ~95:05–100:58.)*

**Why it works** — Natera's interpretation: isometrics raised reactive strength without extra plyometric volume, and position-specific strength carried over into running. Neither interpretation can be separated from other causes in these data.

**When to apply** — Use the sprinter as a **profile template**, not as evidence: high max strength (squat ≥2.5× BW) plus a low RSI and poor max velocity is the athlete Natera would target. In football that is the big, strong accelerator (RB/LB type) whose drop-jump RSI on ForceDecks is low for his strength. Track RSI and single-leg iso push together to see whether one moves without the other.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** Each case is n = 1 with concurrent training: sprint coaching, traditional lifting, technical work and maturation. There is no control, and the selection is plainly of successes. The hurdler also had a new collaborating coach, "great coaching and great technical training," per Natera himself. Elsewhere (~34:19–35:15) he reports programs where RSI was "the only change," and he concedes that is "not exactly a controlled scientific experiment." Do not cite these cases as evidence that RSI improves sprint speed. The 160 kg ankle catch must not become a target.

**Example** — Screening question for a strong but non-reactive athlete: "Is this athlete's RSI low relative to his iso push ×BW?" If yes, he fits the sprinter case, and Natera would add ankle switches and catches after an eccentric calf base.

**Related** — [[principle--isometric-overload-for-upright-running]] — the rationale these cases are offered to illustrate.

14	# The Supercompensation Cycle
15	
16	**What it is** — After a training stimulus the body passes through four phases: (I) fatigue/homeostasis drop, 1–2 hr; (II) compensation/recovery, 24–48 hr; (III) supercompensation — a rebound *above* baseline, ~36–72 hr; (IV) involution — the gain fades if no new stimulus arrives, 3–7 days. Training the next stimulus into the supercompensation window raises the homeostatic set-point over time. Also called Weigert's law; Bompa links it to Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm → resistance → exhaustion).
17	
18	**Why it works** — A bout depletes substrates (glycogen, PCr), accumulates fatigue and cortisol, and transiently lowers force output. Given adequate recovery the body overshoots when restoring those reserves, establishing a new, higher baseline. Protein synthesis is elevated +50% by 4 hr and +109% by 24 hr post-resistance-bout.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Sequencing hard sessions and recovery; justifying why intensities must alternate (high/moderate/low); timing the next stressor to land on the rebound, not the trough.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Don't treat it as a precise single-factor clock. Recovery windows vary enormously by session type (6–8 hr for medium aerobic work; >48 hr for high-CNS work) and by athlete training status, nutrition, and contraction type (eccentric/SSC fatigue recovers bimodally, full recovery 6–8 days). Contemporary sport science largely prefers the **fitness–fatigue (two-factor) model** over literal supercompensation; treat this as a useful mental model, not a measured prescription. See [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]] and [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]].
23	
24	**Example** — After a heavy lower-body session that depletes glycogen and induces DOMS, scheduling the next heavy lower session ~48–72 hr later (not at 24 hr) aims to load the supercompensation rebound rather than residual fatigue.
25

# The Supercompensation Cycle

**What it is** — After a training stimulus the body passes through four phases: (I) fatigue/homeostasis drop, 1–2 hr; (II) compensation/recovery, 24–48 hr; (III) supercompensation — a rebound *above* baseline, ~36–72 hr; (IV) involution — the gain fades if no new stimulus arrives, 3–7 days. Training the next stimulus into the supercompensation window raises the homeostatic set-point over time. Also called Weigert's law; Bompa links it to Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm → resistance → exhaustion).

**Why it works** — A bout depletes substrates (glycogen, PCr), accumulates fatigue and cortisol, and transiently lowers force output. Given adequate recovery the body overshoots when restoring those reserves, establishing a new, higher baseline. Protein synthesis is elevated +50% by 4 hr and +109% by 24 hr post-resistance-bout.

**When to apply** — Sequencing hard sessions and recovery; justifying why intensities must alternate (high/moderate/low); timing the next stressor to land on the rebound, not the trough.

**When NOT to apply** — Don't treat it as a precise single-factor clock. Recovery windows vary enormously by session type (6–8 hr for medium aerobic work; >48 hr for high-CNS work) and by athlete training status, nutrition, and contraction type (eccentric/SSC fatigue recovers bimodally, full recovery 6–8 days). Contemporary sport science largely prefers the **fitness–fatigue (two-factor) model** over literal supercompensation; treat this as a useful mental model, not a measured prescription. See [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]] and [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]].

**Example** — After a heavy lower-body session that depletes glycogen and induces DOMS, scheduling the next heavy lower session ~48–72 hr later (not at 24 hr) aims to load the supercompensation rebound rather than residual fatigue.

14	# Concentrated Loading and Planned Overreaching
15	
16	**What it is** — A short period of deliberately high, "saturated" training load on one quality (planned overreaching), followed by restitution. Performance is *suppressed* during the loading block and rebounds — supercompensates — afterward. Siff and Verkhoshansky note gains may appear **4 to 12 weeks** after the concentrated block ends; the longer/larger the loading, the longer the delay before performance lifts. The **conjugated sequence** extends this: concentrate on one emphasis (e.g. strength) while holding maintenance loads elsewhere, then shift emphasis in the unloading block so a different quality rises.
17	
18	**Why it works** — Saturating a stimulus drives a deeper adaptive signal than steady loading. Monitoring via the **testosterone:cortisol (T:C) ratio** tracks the anabolic–catabolic balance: ≥3 weeks of concentrated load lowers the basal T:C ratio (a catabolic shift, reduced preparedness); returning load to normal lets the T:C ratio and performance supercompensate. T:C indexes *preparedness*, not overtraining per se.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Advanced athletes who can tolerate high loads; building a potent stimulus before a taper/peak; reducing long-term work volume versus concurrent training; timing a delayed performance rebound to a competition window.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Not for novices or athletes without the training capacity to absorb saturating loads — fatigue is substantial during accumulation and mismanagement tips into overtraining. The delayed-rebound timing (4–12 wk) must be planned backward from competition, or the peak lands in the wrong week. Builds on [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--step-loading-paradigm]]; bounded by [[principle--individualization]].
23	
24	**Example** — A 3-week strength-concentrated block (strength up, speed maintained) is timed so the performance rebound surfaces ~4–6 weeks later at the first key competition; T:C ratio is monitored to confirm the post-block recovery.
25

13	
14	# Step Loading (the 3:1 Microcycle Paradigm)
15	
16	**What it is** — The classic periodization loading model: training load rises in a *wavelike* pattern across microcycles rather than continuously. The canonical form is **3:1** — load increases across three microcycles (weeks), then drops in a fourth unloading week for regeneration before the next series begins. Variants scale to the athlete: **4:2** (four loading weeks, two unloading) for more advanced work, **2:1** for younger or less-trained athletes. Because a single session can't drive noticeable adaptation, the load is held across a microcycle, then stepped up.
17	
18	**Why it works** — Loading accumulates fatigue across the three steps; the unloading week sheds fatigue, raises preparedness, and lets the supercompensation/adaptation surface before the next overload (see [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]], [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]). It operationalizes progressive overload safely (see [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]]). The more progressive loading steps, the longer the unloading needed.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Default structure for organizing weeks within a training block; choosing a loading ratio by training age; scheduling deloads on purpose rather than reactively.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Pure **linear loading** (continuous increase, no unloading) only works for short stretches — sustained, it causes overtraining, burnout, and injury. Classic step loading can also create **monotony** if every day of the microcycle repeats the same load; remedy with greater intra- and inter-microcycle variation, or use a **summated microcycle** (each week emphasizes a different quality — strength-endurance, max strength, speed-strength, restoration — reintroduced cyclically), better suited to intermediate/advanced athletes.
23	
24	**Example** — A four-week block runs weeks 1–3 with rising volume/intensity and week 4 as a deload; a developing athlete instead runs a 2:1 pattern so recovery arrives sooner.
25

# Step Loading (the 3:1 Microcycle Paradigm)

**What it is** — The classic periodization loading model: training load rises in a *wavelike* pattern across microcycles rather than continuously. The canonical form is **3:1** — load increases across three microcycles (weeks), then drops in a fourth unloading week for regeneration before the next series begins. Variants scale to the athlete: **4:2** (four loading weeks, two unloading) for more advanced work, **2:1** for younger or less-trained athletes. Because a single session can't drive noticeable adaptation, the load is held across a microcycle, then stepped up.

**Why it works** — Loading accumulates fatigue across the three steps; the unloading week sheds fatigue, raises preparedness, and lets the supercompensation/adaptation surface before the next overload (see [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]], [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]). It operationalizes progressive overload safely (see [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]]). The more progressive loading steps, the longer the unloading needed.

**When to apply** — Default structure for organizing weeks within a training block; choosing a loading ratio by training age; scheduling deloads on purpose rather than reactively.

**When NOT to apply** — Pure **linear loading** (continuous increase, no unloading) only works for short stretches — sustained, it causes overtraining, burnout, and injury. Classic step loading can also create **monotony** if every day of the microcycle repeats the same load; remedy with greater intra- and inter-microcycle variation, or use a **summated microcycle** (each week emphasizes a different quality — strength-endurance, max strength, speed-strength, restoration — reintroduced cyclically), better suited to intermediate/advanced athletes.

**Example** — A four-week block runs weeks 1–3 with rising volume/intensity and week 4 as a deload; a developing athlete instead runs a 2:1 pattern so recovery arrives sooner.

14	# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition
15	
16	**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
17	initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
18	faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
19	(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
20	Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
21	swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
22	same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
23	research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
24	found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
25	and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
26	that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
27	high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
28	performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
29	restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
30	every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
31	pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)
32	
33	**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
34	after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
35	(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
36	a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
37	competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.
38	
39	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
40	of this library's already-captured practical rule
41	([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
42	more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
43	scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
44	coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
45	volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
46	date.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
49	must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
50	periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
51	fitting process. The taper studies cited are from the early-to-mid 1990s and largely from
52	swimming; **Inference:** don't assume the exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to
53	football or other team sports without independent verification.
54	
55	**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
56	keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
57	deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
58	competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
59	shorter fatigue effect clears.
60	
61	**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]],
62	[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)

**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
of this library's already-captured practical rule
([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
date.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
fitting process. The taper studies cited are from the early-to-mid 1990s and largely from
swimming; **Inference:** don't assume the exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to
football or other team sports without independent verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
shorter fatigue effect clears.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]],
[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

14	# The 3:1 Fatigue-to-Fitness Ratio
15	
16	**What it is** — Zatsiorsky and Kraemer (cited by Bompa) propose that the fatigue from a training bout dissipates roughly **three times faster** than the positive training effect persists — e.g., fatigue lasts ~24 hr while the fitness benefit lasts ~72 hr. The positive effect only becomes *visible* once the masking fatigue has cleared; adaptation and improved performance surface afterward.
17	
18	**Why it works** — A session produces two aftereffects with different time courses: a large but short-lived fatigue, and a smaller but longer-lasting fitness gain. Early after the bout, fatigue dominates and hides the gain (the "delayed training effect"); as fatigue decays faster, the net effect turns positive. This is the practical core of the fitness–fatigue (two-factor) model.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Estimating when a quality will "show up" after hard work; spacing testing or competition far enough past a heavy session that fatigue has cleared; explaining why athletes feel worse before they feel better.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — The 3:1 figure is a rule of thumb, not a constant. Training type shifts it — anaerobic work is more fatiguing and lengthens the ratio; CNS-intensive work can extend fatigue well past 24 hr. Don't use it to schedule to the hour. Pairs with [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--three-training-effects]].
23	
24	**Example** — Avoiding a max-strength test in the 24 hr after a heavy, novel eccentric session — waiting ~72 hr so the strength gain is no longer masked by residual fatigue and DOMS.
25

# The 3:1 Fatigue-to-Fitness Ratio

**What it is** — Zatsiorsky and Kraemer (cited by Bompa) propose that the fatigue from a training bout dissipates roughly **three times faster** than the positive training effect persists — e.g., fatigue lasts ~24 hr while the fitness benefit lasts ~72 hr. The positive effect only becomes *visible* once the masking fatigue has cleared; adaptation and improved performance surface afterward.

**Why it works** — A session produces two aftereffects with different time courses: a large but short-lived fatigue, and a smaller but longer-lasting fitness gain. Early after the bout, fatigue dominates and hides the gain (the "delayed training effect"); as fatigue decays faster, the net effect turns positive. This is the practical core of the fitness–fatigue (two-factor) model.

**When to apply** — Estimating when a quality will "show up" after hard work; spacing testing or competition far enough past a heavy session that fatigue has cleared; explaining why athletes feel worse before they feel better.

**When NOT to apply** — The 3:1 figure is a rule of thumb, not a constant. Training type shifts it — anaerobic work is more fatiguing and lengthens the ratio; CNS-intensive work can extend fatigue well past 24 hr. Don't use it to schedule to the hour. Pairs with [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--three-training-effects]].

**Example** — Avoiding a max-strength test in the 24 hr after a heavy, novel eccentric session — waiting ~72 hr so the strength gain is no longer masked by residual fatigue and DOMS.

Chapter 1 
 
 
Block 
periodization  
vs. traditional theory 
 
 
Many generations of scientists, coaches and athletes have tried to build a 
training system that would yield the best performance results. Their efforts have 
focused on three general problems: 
- How to design an effective training plan for a sufficiently long period. 
- How to optimally implement such a plan.                                                            
-     How to achieve the most favorable combination of all athletic abilities exactly 
at the time of the main competition. 
 
These problems belong to training periodization , the purposeful sequencing 
of different training units (long, medium and short-term training cycles and sessions) 
so that the athlete can attain the desired state and planned for results. Because training 
periodization contains many variables and depends on many circumstances, the ideal 
model can exist only in theory. Nevertheless, each year we take another step towards 
more conscious planning and a more complete understanding of training as a whole.  
 
"}, {"page": 13, "text": "2  
 
This chapter summarizes the two most prevalent views of training 
periodization, (a) the traditional approach which has been dominant for a long time, 
and (b) block periodization, which has come into widespread use among high-level 
athletes during the last decades.  
 
1.1. Traditional theory of periodization, basics and limitations 
 
Training periodization was founded during the 1950s in the former USSR and 
was established as a scientific concept by Matveyev in 1964. This theory spread to 
Eastern Europe (Ozolin,1970; Harre,1973) and later to Western countries (Dick, 
1980; Martin, 1980; Bompa, 1984; Yessis, 1987), and constituted a compulsory part 
of training in high-performance sport. In general, periodization exploits the periodic 
changes in human biological and social activities. For a long time, this theory was 
accepted as the universal basis for training in any sport and for athletes on any level of 
competency.  
 
The first criticisms and calls for reform appeared in the early 1980s in elite 
sport as the experience of top coaches stood in contrast to the entrenched theories. 
New approaches proposed by creative coaches and scientists appeared. Extensive 
discussions by sports experts took place in the 1990s in East and West European 
sports magazines. Let us first examine the basics of traditional theory and their 
limitations from the viewpoint of high-performance sport.  
 
1.1.1. The scope of traditional theory  
 
The cornerstones of periodization are formed by a hierarchical system of 
training units that are periodically repeated (Table 1.1). The upper level of the 
hierarchy belongs to the Olympic quadrennial cycle, juxtaposed with other great 
events in the sports world. The next level of the hierarchy is represented by the 
macrocycles. A macrocycle usually lasts one year but can be shortened to half a year 
and even less. This flexibility in the annual cycle subdivision is irrelevant to the block 
periodization approach. The macrocycles are divided into training periods. The 
training periods fulfill a key function in traditional theory because they divide the 
macrocycle into two major parts: the first for more generalized and preliminary work "}, {"page": 14, "text": "3  
 
(preparatory period); (the second for more event-specific work in the specialized pre 
competitive period) and competition (competitive period).  
 
In addition, a third but short period is set aside for active recovery and 
rehabilitation. The next two levels of the hierarchy are reserved for the mesocycles 
(medium-size training cycles) and microcycles (small-size training cycles).  The 
bottom of the hierarchy belongs to workouts and exercises, which are the building 
elements of the entire training system.

The training periods provide sufficient freedom in the training design. 
External factors, such as the competition calendar and seasonal changes, dictate

sequencing, content and duration of the training cycles and define the specifics of the 
means and methods for each training.

mentioned periods and subdivides them into several stages. The training content of 
each stage is very definite with regard to workload volume and intensity (Table 1.2).

1.1.2. Positives and Negatives of the traditional approach 
 
The traditional theory of training athletes was formulated at a time when there 
was limited knowledge and little scientifically proven guidelines for coaching. 
Traditional training periodization, which adopted the up-to-date know-how of the 
1960s, was a breakthrough for coaching and training science. Many of the elements 
postulated then remain valid to this day, including the hierarchical taxonomy and 
terminology of training cycles, the differentiation between general and specialized 
athletic preparation, changes in exercise volume and intensity, basic approaches to 
short-term, medium-term and long-term planning, etc.  It would be unrealistic to 
expect that all of the ideas proposed more than four decades ago would remain 
applicable today. Thus, several of the principles of athletic preparation are not 
important in the alternative Training Block approach.

was postulated in the traditional theory in regard to high level performance.  
Training downplayed the importance of event-specific means during long periods 
of general preparation, where this specificity could be ignored.  Conversely, the

vs. traditional theory 
 
 
Many generations of scientists, coaches and athletes have tried to build a 
training system that would yield the best performance results. Their efforts have 
focused on three general problems: 
- How to design an effective training plan for a sufficiently long period. 
- How to optimally implement such a plan.                                                            
-     How to achieve the most favorable combination of all athletic abilities exactly 
at the time of the main competition. 
 
These problems belong to training periodization , the purposeful sequencing 
of different training units (long, medium and short-term training cycles and sessions) 
so that the athlete can attain the desired state and planned for results. Because training 
periodization contains many variables and depends on many circumstances, the ideal 
model can exist only in theory. Nevertheless, each year we take another step towards 
more conscious planning and a more complete understanding of training as a whole.  
 
"}, {"page": 13, "text": "2  
 
This chapter summarizes the two most prevalent views of training 
periodization, (a) the traditional approach which has been dominant for a long time, 
and (b) block periodization, which has come into widespread use among high-level 
athletes during the last decades.  
 
1.1. Traditional theory of periodization, basics and limitations 
 
Training periodization was founded during the 1950s in the former USSR and 
was established as a scientific concept by Matveyev in 1964. This theory spread to 
Eastern Europe (Ozolin,1970; Harre,1973) and later to Western countries (Dick, 
1980; Martin, 1980; Bompa, 1984; Yessis, 1987), and constituted a compulsory part 
of training in high-performance sport. In general, periodization exploits the periodic 
changes in human biological and social activities. For a long time, this theory was 
accepted as the universal basis for training in any sport and for athletes on any level of 
competency.  
 
The first criticisms and calls for reform appeared in the early 1980s in elite 
sport as the experience of top coaches stood in contrast to the entrenched theories. 
New approaches proposed by creative coaches and scientists appeared. Extensive 
discussions by sports experts took place in the 1990s in East and West European 
sports magazines. Let us first examine the basics of traditional theory and their 
limitations from the viewpoint of high-performance sport.  
 
1.1.1. The scope of traditional theory  
 
The cornerstones of periodization are formed by a hierarchical system of 
training units that are periodically repeated (Table 1.1). The upper level of the 
hierarchy belongs to the Olympic quadrennial cycle, juxtaposed with other great 
events in the sports world. The next level of the hierarchy is represented by the 
macrocycles. A macrocycle usually lasts one year but can be shortened to half a year 
and even less. This flexibility in the annual cycle subdivision is irrelevant to the block 
periodization approach. The macrocycles are divided into training periods. The 
training periods fulfill a key function in traditional theory because they divide the 
macrocycle into two major parts: the first for more generalized and preliminary work "}, {"page": 14, "text": "3

competitive period) and competition (competitive period).  
 
In addition, a third but short period is set aside for active recovery and 
rehabilitation. The next two levels of the hierarchy are reserved for the mesocycles 
(medium-size training cycles) and microcycles (small-size training cycles).  The 
bottom of the hierarchy belongs to workouts and exercises, which are the building 
elements of the entire training system.

1.2. The Block Periodization Concept - general outline 
 
1.2.1. New concepts affecting the rationalize and design of alternative training 
periodization . 
 
In the 1980s, the concept that emerged from prominent coaches pertained to 
what was called, training blocks . This idea was not conceptualized scientifically and 
was open to different interpretations.  However, in its most comprehensive meaning, 
training block  referred to a training cycle of highly concentrated specialized 
workloads. This definition corresponds to the common understanding of the block  as 
an autonomous compact unit of several elements combined for a specific function. 
Further consideration of training blocks as a coaching concept led to several logical 
consequences: "}, {"page": 32, "text": "21 
 
- Highly concentrated training workloads for many qualities cannot be managed 
at the same time.  Therefore, the training block is an alternative to the 
widespread practice of simultaneous complex development of many abilities; 
- Athletic performance in any sport usually demands the mastery of many 
abilities, which, in the case of training blocks, can only be developed 
consecutively, not concurrently; 
- Developing a process that includes morphological, organic and biochemical 
changes requires a sufficiently long time period of about 2-6 weeks, which 
corresponds to the duration of mesocycles.  Hence, training blocks are mostly 
mesocycle-blocks.   
 
One of the most successful coaches to achieve great results using this 
alternative training system was Anatoly Bondarchuk, who coached the gold-, silver-, 
and bronze-medal winners in the hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic 
Games.  He fulfilled the nearly unattainable dream of having the entire Olympic 
podium occupied by athletes of the same coach. Based on his own personal athletic 
experience (he was Olympic hammer throw champion in 1972) and careful 
investigation of throwers’ training programs (as part of his doctoral studies in 1988), 
Bondarchuk created the original periodization chart that completely reformed the 
traditional approaches to training (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988).  
 
Dr. Bondarchuk established three types of specialized mesocycle-blocks: 
developmental , where workload levels gradually increase to maximum; competitive , 
where the load level is stabilized and athletes focus on the competitive performance; 
and restorative , where athletes utilize active recovery and prepare for the next 
developmental program. The duration of the two first types of mesocycles is usually 
four weeks while the third can be shortened to two weeks. The sequencing of these 
blocks depends on the competition schedule and on the responses of individual 
athletes. The outstanding characteristic of this training program design is alternation 
and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block (every four weeks). 
The terms of traditional periodization like “preparatory, competitive and transitory 
periods” were used, but the author noted that in his concept their essence is very 
different.

As already mentioned, the “winds of reformation” became stronger in the 
earlier 1980s. At that time elite USSR canoe-kayak paddlers performed an enormous 
exercise volume.  The prevailing opinion was that this load level was excessive and 
that the training design could be made more effective. The idea of training blocks and 
mesocycle- sequencing was conceptualized, implemented and proved in practice, and 
then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). Three types of mesocycle-blocks were 
elucidated: accumulation , which was devoted to developing basic abilities such as 
general aerobic endurance, muscle strength, and general patterns of movement 
technique; transformation , which focused on developing specific abilities like 
combined aerobic-anaerobic or anaerobic endurance, specialized muscle endurance, 
and event-specific technique; and realization , which was designed as a pre-
competitive training phase that focused mainly on race model exercises, attaining 
maximum speed and recovery prior to the forthcoming competition. 
 
The duration of the mesocycles was established according to physiological and 
biochemical prerequisites that usually allowed four weeks for the accumulation and 
transformation mesocycles, and two weeks for realization. These three mesocycles 
were combined into a separate training stage which ended with competition.  A 
number of training stages formed the annual macrocycle, which was formally 
subdivided into preparatory and competitive periods, but this differentiation was of 
minor importance. 
 
The modified training design allowed for about a 10-15% reduction in the 
annual training volume. Follow-up testing of the national team during preparation 
showed considerable improvement in the main fitness components in all subgroups. 
The radically reformed preparation program resulted in outstanding performances in 
the 1988 Seoul Olympic Games (three gold and three silver medals) and in the 1989 
and 1990 World Championships where eight and nine gold medals, respectively, were 
won. 
 
Another concept affecting the clarification and implementation of the 
alternative preparation approach is the residual training effect (see glossary), a term 
first coined by Brian and James Counsilman (1991). Compared to other types of 
training effects (acute, immediate, cumulative and delayed), residual effect remains 
relatively new and obscure. The residual training effect refers to the retention of "}, {"page": 34, "text": "23 
 
changes induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the 
cessation of training . 
  
The residual training effect phenomenon is closely connected with detraining, 
which was previously understood as a loss of "trainedness" when training was 
stopped. In fact, detraining in high-performance sport usually occurs selectively, 
according to specific abilities when not stimulated by sufficient training. For instance, 
maximum oxygen uptake among highly trained endurance athletes decreases when 
total weekly volume is reduced below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et 
al., 1998). Similarly, large volumes of highly intense exercises do not prevent 
detraining and loss of aerobic endurance during the taper (Mujika, 1999).  
 
When training is designed in the traditional manner and many abilities are 
developed simultaneously, the risk of detraining is negligible because each quality 
(motor or technical ability) receives some portion of the training stimuli. However, if 
these abilities are developed consecutively, as proposed above (Issurin & Kaverin, 
1985, Bondarchuk, 1986, 1988), the problem of detraining becomes very important.  
If you develop one ability and lose another one at the same time, you have to take into 
account the duration of the positive effect of the given training after its cessation and 
how fast you will lose the obtained ability level when you stop training it. In other 
words, you have to know the residual effect of each type of training. A recent study 
presents data summarizing the duration of the training residuals with regard to 
different motor abilities (Table 1.6.)

The rate of loss of the training effects and respective training residuals vary 
widely for different motor abilities. Some physiological systems retain increased 
levels of adaptation longer than others. For example, improved aerobic capacity is 
determined by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, i.e., increases in 
capillary density, glycogen storage and in particular, the amount of aerobic enzymes, 
which increase by 40-90% (Volkov,1986; Fox et al.,1993; Wilmore & Costill, 1993). 
This is in contrast to the much lesser local adaptations seen in athletes after sprint 
training such as increases in phosphocreatine storage (2-5%), peak lactate 
accumulation (10-20%) and anaerobic enzymes (2-20 %). Consequently, aerobic 
ability, which is supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is 
retained for a number of weeks at near-peak level, while anaerobic abilities, "}, {"page": 36, "text": "25 
 
particularly maximum sprint speed, retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods  
(Table 1.6).  
 
Maximum strength gains in top-level athletes are determined by pronounced 
morphological, biochemical and neural changes, such as enlargement of the cross-
sectional area of muscle fibers, increased number of fibers (hyperplasia), recruitment 
of previously inactive motor units and synchronization of their activity, and increased 
discharge frequency of motor-neurons (Zatsiorsky, 1995). All these significant 
adaptations create a relatively long training residual for strength training. 
 
Training residuals of strength endurance are dependent on the duration of the 
event and the degree of mobilization of anaerobic resources.  Strength endurance for 
long-duration performance has relatively longer residuals, thanks to pronounced 
aerobic adaptation.  
 
The changes induced by training for peak speed are characterized by fewer 
gains and shorter residuals. Highly concentrated sprint training causes relatively small 
increases in quickly available energy sources such as ATP and phosphocreatine, and 
enzymes such as creatine kinase (Thorstensson, 1988). In addition, peak speed is 
based on very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which are 
relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially 
organized training.

sport-specific fitness components.  When we stop developing a specific ability we 
should be able to predict how long this ability will remain at the “sufficient” level. 
This information should determine the appropriate sequencing and timing of the 
training cycles.

realize their preparedness as readiness for competition and attain the 
planned result).

most prominent embodiment of the Block Periodization Concept.  They are much 
more concentrated, more specialized, and more manageable in the training programs.

Summary 
 
The traditional theory of training periodization was developed as a universal 
approach to the planning and preparation of athletes. The tremendous changes in 
high-level sport, as well as the dissemination of new training technologies, has led to 
an evolution of general theoretical positions and the appearance of several non-
traditional coaching concepts.  Training Block Periodization, the alternative to the 
traditional preparation approach, reflects the successful experience of many prominent 
coaches and the results of long-term studies conducted on top-level athletes.  
 
The general idea behind the alternative approach is the use of sequenced 
specialized mesocycle-blocks, where highly concentrated training workloads are 
focused on a minimal number of motor and technical abilities. Unlike the traditional 
theory of training periodization that uses simultaneous development of many abilities, 
the alternative concept provides for consecutive development of the targeted abilities 
in successive mesocycle-blocks. The rational sequencing of these blocks is based on 
residual training effects, i.e., the retention of changes brought about by the training 
that remain after the training ceases. These training residuals are especially important 
when athletes improve their abilities consecutively, not concurrently as in the 
traditional model. 
 
The Block Periodization Concept utilizes an original taxonomy of mesocycles 
that consist of three types of specialized blocks: accumulation, for developing basic 
motor and technical abilities (mostly aerobic and muscle strength abilities as well as 
basic technical skills); transmutation, for developing event-specific abilities (mostly 
anaerobic and/or aerobic-anaerobic abilities, and more specialized technical skills), 
and realization , for maximal speed, event-specific tactics and full adaptation prior the 
forthcoming trial or competition (this block is very similar to the widely-known 
concept of pre-event tapering). These three mesocycle-blocks, taken as a whole, form 
the training stage, that is, the most meaningful component of alternative training 
periodization. This contrasts to the classical scheme where the most meaningful 
component is the training period.

Summary 
 
The traditional theory of training periodization was developed as a universal 
approach to the planning and preparation of athletes. The tremendous changes in 
high-level sport, as well as the dissemination of new training technologies, has led to 
an evolution of general theoretical positions and the appearance of several non-
traditional coaching concepts.  Training Block Periodization, the alternative to the 
traditional preparation approach, reflects the successful experience of many prominent 
coaches and the results of long-term studies conducted on top-level athletes.  
 
The general idea behind the alternative approach is the use of sequenced 
specialized mesocycle-blocks, where highly concentrated training workloads are 
focused on a minimal number of motor and technical abilities. Unlike the traditional 
theory of training periodization that uses simultaneous development of many abilities, 
the alternative concept provides for consecutive development of the targeted abilities 
in successive mesocycle-blocks. The rational sequencing of these blocks is based on 
residual training effects, i.e., the retention of changes brought about by the training 
that remain after the training ceases. These training residuals are especially important 
when athletes improve their abilities consecutively, not concurrently as in the 
traditional model. 
 
The Block Periodization Concept utilizes an original taxonomy of mesocycles 
that consist of three types of specialized blocks: accumulation, for developing basic 
motor and technical abilities (mostly aerobic and muscle strength abilities as well as 
basic technical skills); transmutation, for developing event-specific abilities (mostly 
anaerobic and/or aerobic-anaerobic abilities, and more specialized technical skills), 
and realization , for maximal speed, event-specific tactics and full adaptation prior the 
forthcoming trial or competition (this block is very similar to the widely-known 
concept of pre-event tapering). These three mesocycle-blocks, taken as a whole, form 
the training stage, that is, the most meaningful component of alternative training 
periodization. This contrasts to the classical scheme where the most meaningful 
component is the training period.

Chapter 2 
 
The Workout  
General concepts and  
structure guidelines 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Workouts are the smallest complete structural component of a training system.  
When joined and sequenced, workouts form the larger training cycles and stages. The 
current status of workouts is rather contradictory. On the one hand, coaches and 
athletes know how to structure single workouts in their sport. On the other hand, 
training approaches and preparatory schemes are constantly changing and improving.  
As a result, training workouts are modified as well. Some coaches reach a level of 
mastery in their creations, but frequently can not (or do not want to) explain how they 
compiled these sessions. The aim of this chapter is to present the most relevant 
general approaches to structuring the workout. 
 
 
2.1 Workout types and classifications . 
 
This section presents three practical and relevant workout classifications that 
deal with single training sessions in terms of their: (1) organization, (2) training tasks, 
and (3) load level.

use of visual means such as videotapes in order to provide athletes with objective 
information about performance quality and meaningful details about proper technique.

requires high mobilization of athletes' cognitive and coordinative abilities. Therefore, 
this workout type causes a particularly heavy load on the athletes’ central nervous 
system that should be taken into account during planning.

new tactical skills and the perfection of individual and/or team tactics. Another 
function of these workouts is to link tactical and technical skills, which is extremely 
important for successful performance. Several parts of tactical workouts can be 
practiced in sessions as part of theoretical and mental preparation. However, the major 
part of this work should be planned and thoroughly implemented in sport-specific 
conditions where stressful competitive situations can be partially simulated. This type 
of workout is more characteristic of team and combat sports, where the importance of 
tactics is relatively higher.

technical abilities with regard to specially selected components of preparedness

approach conditions in the forthcoming event as closely as possible. As these sessions 
demand maximal efforts from athletes, this type of workout should be carefully 
arranged and provided with the appropriate equipment in a suitable environment and 
with full cooperation of the coaching staff.

perfection of appropriate technical skills. These combined training means, having a 
two-sided effect, are termed conjugate exercises . Usually such conjugation is 
provided in the form of speed resisted and speed assisted exercises (Maglischo, 1992).  
They can also be done with specialized strength exercises (Yessis, 2006)

popular in cyclic type sports such as running, swimming, canoeing, rowing etc.

sport-specific technical skill and enhancing appropriate muscular endurance. The 
speed resisted approach can usually be realized with the help of relatively 
inexpensive equipment. Speed assisted exercises are supposed to facilitate high 
speed regimes and often, to break the so-called “speed barrier”. The combined 
effect of such drills is the enhancement of sport-specific speed technique and 
improvement of maximal speed or event-specific speed endurance.

differentiation of workouts is of particular importance. For practical purposes, it is 
necessary to enumerate three general functions of workouts: development, retention

In actual fact, each training plan is a specific combination of these workout types: 
some are intended to enhance development, others are necessary to retain certain 
capabilities at the previously attained level; and special sessions are planned for 
restoration. Therefore, the aim related workout load classification has practical value. 
Zatsiorsky's load-related classification (1995), presents quantified workouts on a scale 
of 1 to 5 where 1 represents the lowest load and 5 the highest, as seen in Table 2.3.

of the training composed of several workouts.  The principle of high concentration

number of development workouts as the crucial factor.  
 
Example . A highly qualified canoeist needs to develop basic aerobic endurance. 
For this purpose he has to perform a 40-45 km weekly volume of exercises at 
near- anaerobic threshold level. Following the traditional approach, this mileage 
can be divided among nine workouts, where these exercises will be combined 
with drills for other training modalities (anaerobic glycolitic endurance, strength 
endurance, maximal speed etc.). The athlete performing this program will be 
permanently fatigued and the training effect will be small to negligible.   
 
The BPC requires concentration on target-specific exercises mostly within 
three-four development workouts that can not be combined with any anaerobic 
glycolitic tasks. The athletes will sometimes (but not always) be fatigued after 
strenuous development workouts, but the training effect will be more favorable.   
 
According to the BPC, quality of training is determined strictly by the quantity 
and placement of development workouts. Moreover, some of the workouts should be 
especially stressed and carefully arranged through appropriate planning. The most 
important development workouts, which are focused on the current main training 
emphasis, are called “ key-workouts ”.

which create peak points of related training cycles and concentrate the most important 
tasks and workloads.  Such   peak sessions, recently renamed “key-workouts”, require 
athletes to concentrate mentally and emotionally and to be ready to work harder than 
usual. 
 
Example . Tim Noakes (1991), a well known sport physiologist, formulated a 
number of training rules based on the experiences of the greatest middle- and 
long-distance runners  such as Herbert Elliott, Ron Clarke and Frank Shorter. The 
first one is: “Alternate hard and easy training days”. This is very similar to the 
coaching concept of key-workout, which can be expressed as, “alternate 
particularly stressful workouts with less hard and easy sessions”.

2.2 Workout structure  
 
Despite the variety and specificity of various sports, there are general rules 
about how each single workout should be structured. Knowledge of workout structure 
relates to the most comprehensive part of training theory, which all coaches begin to 
learn from their initial experiences in their athletic career. Indeed, everyone knows 
that a single workout consists of a warm-up  (introductory part), basic part  where 
planned workloads are performed, and cool-down  (concluding part). This general 
structure pertains to all possible combinations of organizational forms and exercises 
and has been described by many authors. Nevertheless, progress in sports science and 
practice has led to a more complete understanding of the facts which once seemed 
very simple but now appear more sophisticated. Thus, the essence and content of each 
workout component can now be elucidated with greater clarity. 
 
2.2.1 Warm-up  
 
 The great New Zealand coach Arthur Lydiard include d a chapter on warm-up 
in his book with Garth Gilmour (2000). He mentioned that world renowned 
Australian coach Percy Cerutty, who had worked with multiple world record holder 
and Olympic running champion Herbert Elliott, was asked about the role of warm-up. 
The authoritative coach answered that rabbits don’t warm-up but can run “like the 
very devil”. The anonymous coach from Abilene  College who had asked the question 
took this reply seriously and conducted a special study. 
 
Case study.  The Abilene coach filmed a rabbit’s behavior prior to its 
running activity. When rabbit came out from its burrow, it looked around 
(moving its head and stretching its neck and back muscles) and trotted forth 
and back several times. Afterwards the rabbit started to run across the field. 
Thus, the rabbit really performed a warm-up although not as seriously as 
human runners (Lydiard & Gilmour, 2000). 
   
It would be fair to say that nowadays, very few coaches or athletes still doubt 
the necessity of warming up. However, examples of effective models and 
combinations are required. To this end, as is usual in high-performance training, two 
major approaches exist: summarizing experiences from around the world, and "}, {"page": 58, "text": "47
