illustrated by the findings of a long-term study conducted with high-level athletes. 
 
 
Case study.  Twelve National division soccer teams (180 players) were 
subdivided into two groups. The first one used a modified training program 
where warm-ups and cool-downs were carefully conducted, based on the 
outcomes of previous studies.  This included ball exercises combined with a 
stretching program and cool-downs that consisted of jogging and hold-relax 
stretching. The preparation was supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. 
The second group of six teams trained traditionally and served as the 
control. The results of a six month follow up revealed highly significant 
superiority for the modified preparation program (Figure 2.1). There was a 
four-fold reduction in the number of injuries and a drastic decrease in 
workouts and games missed due to musculoskeletal disorders (Ekstrand et 
al, 1983).   
 
The above study can be considered atypical because it refers to the complex 
effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision. Usually the scientific 
approach deals with the separate effects of several factors and what their outcomes 
can contribute to practice. For instance: 
- incorporating stretching exercises in the warm-up increases the range of 
motion of soccer players' lower extremities (Moller et al., 1985); 
- active warm-up without stretching doesn’t affect flexibility and is therefore 
insufficient (Zakas et al., 2006); 
- prior intense exercise substantially stimulates aerobic metabolism in working 
muscles during subsequent strenuous performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). 
On the other hand, experiences in advanced sports practice remain a very 
valuable source for organizing warm-up in a particular sport.

The basic part of the workout is sometimes called the “loading phase” because 
it concentrates all the real workloads planned for the session. Thus, the desired acute

performance time, movement rate etc.), and subjective signs of effort and/or fatigue

attainment and maintenance of the highest level for this session. The basic part is the 
longest one in the workout and usually lasts about 60-90 min. Of course, during this 
time interval, the load level should be properly adjusted.

exercise or task. The coaches termed this “the meaningful exercise”, “the chief link of

workout. Obviously, a workout program for runners does not contain only one 
exercise; what Lydiard did was to pinpoint only the most important one.  
Similarly, typical weekly training reports of great running stars display one 
exercise in each workout which means that the athletes report only on exercises or 
drills of primary importance (Noakes, 1991)

Chapter 2 
 
The Workout  
General concepts and  
structure guidelines 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Workouts are the smallest complete structural component of a training system.  
When joined and sequenced, workouts form the larger training cycles and stages. The 
current status of workouts is rather contradictory. On the one hand, coaches and 
athletes know how to structure single workouts in their sport. On the other hand, 
training approaches and preparatory schemes are constantly changing and improving.  
As a result, training workouts are modified as well. Some coaches reach a level of 
mastery in their creations, but frequently can not (or do not want to) explain how they 
compiled these sessions. The aim of this chapter is to present the most relevant 
general approaches to structuring the workout. 
 
 
2.1 Workout types and classifications . 
 
This section presents three practical and relevant workout classifications that 
deal with single training sessions in terms of their: (1) organization, (2) training tasks, 
and (3) load level.

a number of similarly ranked athletes train together.  This is the prevailing form in 
team and combat sports. It should be noted that long-term preparation using group

When athletes train with high motivation, competitiveness and prolonged emotional 
strain, it can lead to excessive and chronic excitation of the central nervous system 
and eventually to emotional exhaustion. This is why it is essential to find a 
harmonious blend of strictly programmed team workouts here and in other types of 
workouts.

liberal and less strenuous preparation.  The use of individual workouts is greater in 
individual sports than in team and combat sports. In several sports like figure skating, 
individual workouts form almost the entire preparatory program of highly qualified 
athletes. Nevertheless, even in team sports, individual workouts contribute to the 
program of preparation as a whole. In soccer, basketball, ice hockey etc. pre-season 
preparation of world-class players is their own responsibility. World-class stars have 
to find their own facilities, coaching assistance and workout time-tables, which are 
usually individualized. 
 
 
Example . A highly successful, professional soccer player underwent a one-month 
specialized mesocycle for maximum speed during the off-season when 30-33 
years old. He engaged a highly qualified track and field sprint coach, who

2.2.3 Cooling down  
 
 The last, but still compulsory part of each single  workout is intended to reduce 
load level gradually and normalize basic functions in the body.  It is called the cool-
down . Its specific objectives are: 
- to reduce body temperature, heart rate and blood pressure back to resting 
levels; 
- to remove acid metabolites and other waste products from the muscles to the 
circulatory system for further clearance; 
- to facilitate recovery of the endocrine system first, by reducing adrenaline and 
noradrenaline levels in order to prevent restlessness and sleep disorders at 
night; 
- to reduce emotional tension and affect athletes' mental recovery in a positive 
way. 
 
Generally speaking, the cool-down is both an influencing factor and a relevant 
condition for effective restoration of the athlete. Despite its obvious importance there 
have been many cases in which this indispensable part of the workout has been 
ignored, even by successful high-performance athletes. Usually a lack of time is cited 
as the reason for such mistaken behavior. The previously mentioned study of 
professional soccer players (Figure 2.2) has shown the role of rational warm-up and 
cool-down in protecting the athletes' health. As further support, the following study 
outcomes can be cited.

Exercises for strength endurance and aerobic endurance demand sustained 
efforts despite accumulated fatigue and should therefore be continued as long as 
possible. The general rule is that motor learning demands an optimal state of the CNS 
and energy resourses.  However, several technical features can be improved in highly 
exhausting workloads. For instance, fatigue tolerance of motor skill, movement 
economy and technique stability in unfavorable fatigue conditions can be enhanced

stretching exercises are recommended for use in any part of the workout.  It can be at

improving flexibility, and at the end as a component of cool-down.

defined dominant ability targeted for the session.  It in turn determines the content and 
placement of the key-exercise. Sometimes even small variations in the exercise order 
can modify and even suppress the expected acute effect. This can be illustrated using 
for example, high-resistance training, an indispensable part of the program for many 
sports.

performing the squats first. The authors attributed this phenomenon to

hypertrophy should plan this exercise for the initial part of workout.  If the main

Workouts often seem to be a trivial and simple component of the training 
system that require no special consideration or clarification.  But, the Block 
Periodization approach emphasizes several aspects of workout structure that were "}, {"page": 82, "text": "71 
 
ignored or insufficiently considered previously.  For example, the proposed aim-load 
related classification offers a distinction among three different workout types: 
development, which provides the major training stimuli for progress, retention that is 
aimed at maintaining several abilities at the level attained, and restoration, which 
facilitates recovery after the preceding high-load sessions. The proposed five-point 
scale enables coaches to quantify workouts according to load in any sport, where one 
point indicates the minimal level and five points – extreme workloads. Based on the 
experience of prominent coaches the term “ key-workout ” was proposed and 
explained. It stresses the most important development workouts that are focused on 
the main training objective and help facilitate the key-function. 
   
Warm-up and cool-down are considered indispensable structural elements of a 
workout. This chapter stressed the role of warm-up in metabolic and technical 
adjustment, mental readiness and prevention of injuries. Similarly, the cool-down was 
considered from the viewpoint of restoration and injury prevention. The basic part of 
the workout was described with regard to the main content element which was termed 
the key-exercise or key-task . The methodological, psycho-physiological and 
organizational aspects of the key-exercise are also presented.

 The format of this chapter and entire book does no t allow a thorough 
consideration of the above schematic description of key-exercises. In addition, very

2.2.3 Cooling down  
 
 The last, but still compulsory part of each single  workout is intended to reduce 
load level gradually and normalize basic functions in the body.  It is called the cool-
down . Its specific objectives are: 
- to reduce body temperature, heart rate and blood pressure back to resting 
levels; 
- to remove acid metabolites and other waste products from the muscles to the 
circulatory system for further clearance; 
- to facilitate recovery of the endocrine system first, by reducing adrenaline and 
noradrenaline levels in order to prevent restlessness and sleep disorders at 
night; 
- to reduce emotional tension and affect athletes' mental recovery in a positive 
way. 
 
Generally speaking, the cool-down is both an influencing factor and a relevant 
condition for effective restoration of the athlete. Despite its obvious importance there 
have been many cases in which this indispensable part of the workout has been 
ignored, even by successful high-performance athletes. Usually a lack of time is cited 
as the reason for such mistaken behavior. The previously mentioned study of 
professional soccer players (Figure 2.2) has shown the role of rational warm-up and 
cool-down in protecting the athletes' health. As further support, the following study 
outcomes can be cited.

Case study . Forty-eight adult soccer players were subdivided into three groups 
that were tested with respect to range of motion (ROM) in the lower extremities 
before, immediately after, and 24 h after different types of workouts. The regular 
soccer workout caused a significant decrease in all ROM indices. A similar 
workout that included a stretching series in warm-up induced more favorable 
responses immediately after the session. The third version, in which the stretching 
series was inserted in the cool down, provided significant benefits in ROM 
immediately after the workout and 24 h later. The authors stressed that tight 
muscles with reduced ROM predisposed the athletes to a higher risk of injuries 
(Moller et al., 1985).  
 
 
 In general, the cool-down repertory can be subdivi ded into three categories: 
(1) low intensity exercises, usually slow locomotions like jogging, walking, 
swimming etc., (2) breathing and relaxation exercises and (3) stretching exercises.  
The particulars of these activities are summarized in Table 2.11.   
 
The common pattern of cool-down usually starts with slow locomotion that 
leads to elimination of waste products from the muscles. It has long been known that 
such activity facilitates recovery and causes faster lactate removal from the athlete's 
muscles (Bonen & Belcastro, 1976). It is known that highly intense and prolonged 
exercises cause a decrease in circulating blood volume due to water accumulation in 
intra- and extra-cellular compartments of the muscles (Sejersted et al., 1986). 
Recovery of the water-electrolyte balance may take a long time.  In extreme cases 
(marathon running, for instance) it can reach two or more days (Viru, 1995). An 
effecitve cool-down procedure can profoundly accelerate this process.

eliminating post-exercise muscle stiffness and tightness, and enhancing muscle and

be insufficient when the workout consists of a number of high intensity anaerobic 
sets.  Cooling down usually lasts about 10-20 minutes which is not enough after 
sessions with extreme workloads.

coach develops his/her own style based on personal experiences and accumulated 
knowledge. Therefore, there are a variety of versions even within a given sport. At the

Both warm-up and cool-down can be 
modified according to workout specific 
demands

equipment and workout 
conditions 
Monitoring means, training machines, 
accessories and as far as possible, weather 
conditions, should be checked 
  
It may not be necessary to prepare a full description of each workout with all 
the details mentioned in the table, but all details should be taken into account. It is 
highly recommended to familiarize the athletes with the upcoming workout plan. 
World famous swim coach and sport scientist James Counsilman (1968) used to write 
the workout content on a large blackboard in front of the swimming pool. It was his 
contention that this definitely increases motivation and affects the consciousness 
needed to perform heavy workloads. In general, coaches should be ready to explain to 
curious athletes why they selected certain combinations of exercises and not others.

Workouts often seem to be a trivial and simple component of the training 
system that require no special consideration or clarification.  But, the Block 
Periodization approach emphasizes several aspects of workout structure that were "}, {"page": 82, "text": "71

related classification offers a distinction among three different workout types: 
development, which provides the major training stimuli for progress, retention that is 
aimed at maintaining several abilities at the level attained, and restoration, which 
facilitates recovery after the preceding high-load sessions. The proposed five-point 
scale enables coaches to quantify workouts according to load in any sport, where one 
point indicates the minimal level and five points – extreme workloads. Based on the 
experience of prominent coaches the term “ key-workout ” was proposed and 
explained. It stresses the most important development workouts that are focused on 
the main training objective and help facilitate the key-function.

adjustment, mental readiness and prevention of injuries. Similarly, the cool-down was

the workout was described with regard to the main content element which was termed

organizational aspects of the key-exercise are also presented.

minimization of training modalities within a workout as follows: one dominant 
modality, a second one that is compatible with the main objective, and a third one to 
improve technique/tactics or provide restoration. Usually 65-70 % of all training time

modalities. Compatible combinations of different training modalities within single

can embrace two-six sessions. Factors such as load sequencing, exercise compatibility

13	
14	# Bondarchuk's Four Exercise Categories, Applied to Sprinting
15	
16	**What it is** — The classic three-way split (general preparatory / special preparatory / competitive, in use for "more than 100 years" per Moyer) was refined by Bondarchuk into four classes, each defined by how much of the competition movement it reproduces:
17	
18	| Class | Definition (as Moyer gives it) | Sprint examples from the course |
19	|---|---|---|
20	| **General preparatory (GPE)** | Resembles no part of the competition movement; for all-round conditioning and recovery | General conditioning, recovery work |
21	| **Special preparatory (SPE)** | Does not copy the event's movement but trains the same muscle groups and physiological systems | Max strength, Olympic lifts, jumps, med-ball throws. **The clean goes here.** Moyer says sprinting has no "triple extension", so a clean's recruitment resembles sprinting but its movement does not |
22	| **Special developmental (SDE)** | Repeats part or all of the competition event, usually against resistance | Band-resisted knee drive, band-resisted pawback, bounding, "ball under" knee-drive work |
23	| **Competition (CE)** | The whole event, with lighter or heavier loads | Sprinting itself; sprinting with light wearable resistance; (by analogy) throwing lighter balls |
24	
25	**Why it works** — It puts the theory of identical elements into practice (see [[principle--sprint-transfer-motor-ability-vs-motor-skill]]). The further down the table, the more elements the exercise shares with the sprint and the higher the chance of *skill* transfer. The higher up the table, the more the exercise builds general capacity with skill transfer unlikely. Bondarchuk's refinement matters because he found parts of "general" and "special" work can still transfer depending on the block and the athlete. Moyer asserts the mechanism. The data behind it are Bondarchuk's, and the course only summarises them.
26	
27	**When to apply** — Auditing a college football speed/strength program: label every exercise GPE/SPE/SDE/CE and check the mix fits the phase. In summer you might expect SPE-heavy work with some SDE. In fall camp, CE (sprinting) and SDE should lead. In RTP after a hamstring strain, the classes give a ready progression: GPE/SPE for tissue capacity → SDE (banded pawback, isometric hamstring work in sprint positions) → CE (sprinting, then sprinting with light external load).
28	
29	**When NOT to apply** — The classes describe *movement* similarity only. They say nothing about perceptual similarity. A CE-class 40-yard sprint is still decontextualised from game running, where a receiver sprints relative to a DB and a ball (see the Myszka entries). Class boundaries are fuzzy. Moyer's "no triple extension in sprinting" is a contested biomechanics claim being used to place the clean in a class. And the table does not tell you the *dose* of each class. That is the separate unification principle.
30	
31	**Example** — A wideout's June week: trap-bar and hang clean (SPE), banded knee-drive and pawback (SDE), and wicket runs plus flying sprints (CE). In August the SPE volume drops and the CE share rises, but no class disappears.
32	
33	**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-adaptation]] — agree that later phases sharpen toward the competition movement; Moyer's four classes give a finer grain than Bompa's general→specific sequence.

14	# Immediate, Delayed, and Cumulative Training Effects
15	
16	**What it is** — A training program produces effects on three timescales: **Immediate** — the acute physiological reaction during and right after a session (↑heart rate, ↑blood pressure, ↓force from fatigue, glycogen depletion). **Delayed** — the lasting positive benefit that appears only *after* the session's fatigue dissipates; the more intense the bout, the longer until the gain is realized. **Cumulative** — the compounding result of many sessions or phases, including threshold-breaking blocks, which can produce a surprising jump in performance ("we worked hard and suddenly it just happened").
17	
18	**Why it works** — Each session leaves a short-lived acute disturbance and a longer-lived adaptive residue. Good planning — alternating high loads with compensation sessions — lets delayed effects surface and lets residues stack into the cumulative effect. The overall outcome is shaped by current training state, prior bouts, and the order/spacing of all stimuli.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Setting expectations for *when* gains appear; reassuring during a hard block that suppressed performance is the immediate effect masking a delayed gain; explaining peaking, where a cumulative effect is unmasked by reduced load.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Don't judge a program by immediate-effect readings alone (a fatigued, depressed test mid-block is expected, not failure). The cumulative effect requires deliberate alternation of load and recovery — pile on intensity without compensation and you get overtraining, not a rebound. See [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] and [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]].
23	
24	**Example** — An athlete's vertical jump dips through a heavy three-week block (immediate effect), then rebounds above baseline during a deload as the delayed and cumulative effects surface.
25

13	
14	# Specificity of Adaptation
15	
16	**What it is** — Adaptation is highly specific to the type of training undertaken. Training must therefore be built around the **energy systems**, **skills**, and **motor abilities** that dominate the target sport. The structural and physiological changes a body makes are dictated by the specific demands the athlete imposes — via the volume, intensity, and frequency of the activities pursued.
17	
18	**Why it works** — Different stressors drive distinct adaptations: neuromuscular (motor-unit recruitment, firing rate, hypertrophy), metabolic (ATP/PCr/glycogen stores, lactate tolerance, glycolytic vs oxidative efficiency), and cardiorespiratory (stroke volume, capillary density, lactate threshold, V̇O₂max). You get back the specific quality you trained; the more complex the sport, the longer adaptation takes.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Exercise and modality selection; justifying why general fitness must eventually yield to sport-specific work; matching the bioenergetic emphasis of a block to competition demands.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Specificity is not a mandate to train *only* the competition movement from day one — that conflicts with building a broad base first (see [[principle--multilateral-before-specialization]]). Early over-specialization narrows the foundation and raises injury risk. Specificity governs the *later*, sharper phases; the general-to-specific sequence still holds.
23	
24	**Example** — A team-sport athlete needing repeated-sprint ability trains the glycolytic/PCr systems with short high-intensity intervals and change-of-direction work, rather than steady-state aerobic runs that would adapt the wrong energy system.
25

12	---
13	
14	# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept
15	
16	**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
17	to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
18	acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
19	the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
20	strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
21	peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
22	below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
23	cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
24	(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
25	anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
26	recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
27	circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
28	older term "anaerobic threshold" has similarly been replaced by "blood lactate threshold"
29	or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation) since lactate does not require an absence of
30	oxygen to form. (PDF pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)
31	
32	**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
33	physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
34	product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
35	rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
36	dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).
37	
38	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
39	classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
40	next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
41	framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is

# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept

**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
older term "anaerobic threshold" has similarly been replaced by "blood lactate threshold"
or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation) since lactate does not require an absence of
oxygen to form. (PDF pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
"flushing out lactic acid."

**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

25	different timelines). Overtraining specifically shows a distinct pattern: reduced

34	late and lost early.

12	---
13	
14	# Muscle Adapts in Days; Tendon, Ligament, and Bone Take Weeks to Months
15	
16	**What it is** — Muscle tissue adapts to increased loading within several days, whereas
17	connective tissues (tendon, ligament, joint capsule) and tissue systems with a high
18	connective-tissue content (bone, cartilage) only show significant adaptation and
19	hypertrophy after several weeks to months of progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies,
20	1984). Verkhoshansky states training prescription must account for the different
21	adaptation rates of all involved systems and avoid overtraining whichever system adapts
22	slowest; he recommends gradual load increases and avoiding impulsive/explosive methods
23	particularly during General Physical Preparation (GPP) and for relative novices to
24	strength training. (PDF p. 46, printed p. 35.)
25	
26	**Why it works** — Muscle's adaptive machinery (protein synthesis, neural recruitment)
27	responds faster than the slower turnover and remodeling of collagenous tissue; a program
28	that progresses load at the muscle's adaptation rate can outpace what tendon, ligament,
29	and bone can structurally tolerate, which is a well-established mechanism in tendon and
30	connective-tissue injury research independent of this text.
31	
32	**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly supports conservative, gradual load
33	progression in GPP/early training blocks and for novice athletes specifically, and argues
34	against introducing high-impulse plyometric or explosive work before a base period of
35	progressive loading has given connective tissue time to adapt. This is a mechanistic
36	rationale for why "the athlete feels ready for more" (muscle-level readiness) is not
37	sufficient justification for a rapid load jump (tendon/bone-level readiness lags behind).
38	
39	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this passage gives no specific timeline (only
40	"several days" vs. "several weeks or months") and no athlete-population-specific data; do
41	not treat it as a precise dosing table. **Inference:** this is a general injury-risk
42	mechanism, not a substitute for clinical input from Athletic Medicine on a specific
43	athlete's tissue status or injury history.
44	
45	**Example** — **Inference:** a novice athlete whose squat strength (muscle-level) is
46	progressing quickly should still have their loading ramp paced by a longer timeline
47	(weeks to months) appropriate to tendon and bone adaptation, not by how fast their 1RM is
48	climbing.
49	
50	**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].
51

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) defines three related but distinct
terms. Work capacity is the general ability of the body to produce work of different
intensity and duration using its energy systems. Fitness is the specific ability to use
that work capacity to execute a given task efficiently and safely; it is a slow-changing
state that does not vary meaningfully over a period of days. Preparedness is not stable:
it is the resultant, at any given instant, of the interaction between the slow-changing
fitness component and the fast-changing, opposing effect of exercise-induced fatigue.

sickness, fatigue, sleepiness) without any change in underlying fitness. (PDF pp. 43-44,
printed pp. 32-33; developed further at 1.16.3.)

**Why it works** — Separating a slow, structural capacity (fitness) from a fast,
state-dependent expression of it (preparedness) explains why an athlete's fitness can be
objectively unchanged from one day to the next while their measured or perceived output
still swings substantially, because the fatigue component is riding on top of a stable
base.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical
capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness
(day-to-day fluctuation) in the department's own testing philosophy, with both tracked
because they answer different questions (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment,"

"preparedness," Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" ~ the baseline's "readiness"), though the
two sources use the words differently and neither cites the other; a reader moving between
them should track the underlying concept, not the label.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the terminology mismatch matters — do not assume
"preparedness" means the same thing in both sources without checking which sense is
meant, since Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" is the department's "readiness," not its

1	[{"page": 44, "text": "33 
 
It should be noted that the traditional approach has visible benefits for the 
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes. The complex administration of workloads 
directed at many abilities makes training more diversified, attractive and lively. The 
improvement of relatively lower athletic abilities doesn’t require highly concentrated 
training workloads because medium-level concentration still provides sufficient 
stimulation. The opposite situation is typical for high-level athletes who need high 
concentrations of appropriate exercises in order to make progress. Table 1.8 presents 
the main differences between the traditional and alternative training models.  
 
The benefits of the Block Periodization Concept, in comparison to the 
traditional model, are as follows:  
(1) the total volume of training exercises can be greatly reduced, minimizing 
the incidence of overtraining,  
(2) the multi-peak training design allows for and facilitates successful 
participation in multiple competitions over the entire season;  
(3) monitoring can be more efficient because of the substantial reduction in the 
number of athletic abilities to be evaluated within each mesocycle;  
(4) the diet and restorative program can be appropriately modified according 
to the predominant type of training and, finally,  
(5) a multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in 
time for the main competition of the season.   
 
 
 "}]
2

content.content:
1	[{"page": 25, "text": "14 
 
 
 
Study and example.  A group of highly qualified kayakers was studied during 
their yearly preparation designed on the classical model. The incremental pattern step 
test was used to determine velocity at anaerobic threshold ((V-AT) and mean distance 
velocity in all-out performance (Vd). Peak Force on the paddle (PF) and Stroke Rate 
(SR) were obtained with the help of a portable telemetry system. Anthropometric 
measurements made it possible to calculate muscle mass (MM).  As can be seen in 
Fig.1.3, the long period of general preparation (preparatory period) caused a 
substantial increase in aerobic endurance (V-AT), muscle mass and strength (peak 
force on the paddle).  
During the relatively long period of highly specialized competition, extensive 
aerobic workloads were replaced by more intense event-specific exercises.  Maximum 
strength exercises were reduced and even rejected as harmful for racing technique. As 
a result, the velocity at anaerobic threshold and peak force decreased during the 
competitive period, and muscle mass diminished prior to competition. It is worth 
noting that mean distance velocity reached maximum for the main competition, 
obtained by the increased stroke rate despite reduced force application to the paddle. 
It is obvious that the timing pattern for developing different abilities was far from 
optimal (Issurin et al., 1986). 
 
 "}]
2

# Block Periodization: Breakthrough in Sport Training (Issurin, 2008) — ingest map

PDF is real text: 221 pages, `extract_pdf.py --probe`: `{"pages": 221, "text_pages": 221,
"scanned": false}`. Publisher: Ultimate Athlete Concepts, 2008.

**Print-to-PDF page offset = +11** (PDF page = printed page + 11). Verified at five
independent chapter starts, not just the offset's origin point: Ch1 (printed 1 = PDF 12,
"Block periodization vs. traditional theory"), Ch2 (printed 36 = PDF 47, "The Workout:
general concepts and structure guidelines"), Ch3 (printed 76 = PDF 87, "Microcycles,
mesocycles and training stages"), Ch4 (printed 125 = PDF 136, "Long-term preparation"),
Ch5 (printed 160 = PDF 171, "Altitude training"). Glossary starts printed 202 = PDF 213.
The offset holds unchanged front matter through at least PDF 213 of 221; no evidence of a
mid-book repagination.

**Note on the extractor's `--pages A-B` flag:** the upper bound is exclusive (returns pages
A..B-1). Two pages were missed on the first pass of Chapter 1 (PDF 25 and 44) and recovered
with a follow-up call before atomizing; watch for this on later chapters.

**Confidence rule for this book:** `proven` is reserved for physiology/mechanics established
independent of this text (e.g. CNS fatigue and motor-unit recruitment order, connective
tissue/warm-up basics already `proven` elsewhere in this library). Issurin's own periodization
theory, block-sequencing prescriptions, and the numeric tables he or his co-authors derived
(residual-effect durations, key-exercise interval tables, the ≤3-modality/65-70% workout rule)
are capped at `supported`: they are a single author's synthesis of Soviet/Israeli
sport-science practice and secondary citations, not independently replicated in this ingest.
Single-case coaching anecdotes (Bondarchuk's podium sweep, the author's own 1985 canoe-kayak
program, the Gal Friedman example) are `untested`. `contested` is set where this text
conflicts with a claim already in this library, named explicitly both ways. Issurin's own
later peer-reviewed review — "Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training
Approaches to Athletes' Preparation" (Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, Zotero item
`PT9QTQ2I`) — is in the user's Zotero library but full text is not yet cached for this
ingest; entries below flag where that review would likely qualify a 2008 claim, without
citing content from it that hasn't been read.

| # | Chapter | Printed pp | PDF idx | Status | Entries |
|---|---------|-----------|---------|--------|---------|
| 1 | Block Periodization vs. traditional theory | 1-35 | 12-46 | done | 8 |
| 2 | The Workout: general concepts and structure guidelines | 36-73 | 47-84 | done | 9 |
| 3 | Microcycles, mesocycles and training stages | 76-124 | 87-135 | pending | 0 |
| 4 | Long-term preparation | 125-159 | 136-170 | pending | 0 |
| 5 | Altitude training | 160-201 | 171-212 | pending | 0 |
| — | Glossary / About the author | 202-end | 213-221 | skip | n/a (reference matter, not atomized) |

**Chapter 1 section map** (for locator precision): 1.1 Traditional theory (printed 1-20,
PDF 12-31); 1.2 The Block Periodization Concept (printed 20-31, PDF 31-42, contains the
accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy and Table 1.6 residual-effect durations);
1.3 Consequences of the modern approach (printed 31-33, PDF 42-44); Summary (printed 32-33,
PDF 43-44); References (printed 34-35, PDF 45-46, not atomized).

**Chapter 2 section map**: 2.1 Workout classifications (printed 36-45, PDF 47-56); 2.2
Workout structure — warm-up/main/cool-down (printed 46-59, PDF 57-70); 2.3 Guidelines for
constructing a workout — sequencing, compatibility, daily series (printed 60-69, PDF 71-80);
2.4 How to structure a workout / Summary (printed 69-72, PDF 80-83); References (printed 73,
PDF 84, not atomized).

_Batch 1 (this session): built the chapter map and atomized Chapters 1-2, per the ingest
review gate's two-stage process — stopping cleanly at the Chapter 2/3 boundary so the
Codex falsification review (`staging/review_block-periodization-issurin_codex.md`) can run
on a complete, self-contained unit before Chapter 3 begins._

_Batch 2 (recommended next): Chapter 3 alone (PDF 87-135, printed 76-124, ~49 printed pages).
This is the chapter the strength-and-conditioning miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for
collegiate football") most needs — it covers microcycle types (3.1, including the
pre-competitive/tuning microcycle at 3.1.6), the accumulation/transmutation/realization
mesocycles in full prescriptive detail (3.2, only introduced at a conceptual level in Ch1),
and "how to prolong the residual training effects" (3.3.2) directly. Recommend NOT combining
with Chapter 4 in the same batch — Ch3 alone is already comparable in density to Ch1+Ch2
combined (Table-heavy, multiple sub-mesocycle types per microcycle category)._

_Batch 3 (after Ch3): Chapter 4, Long-term preparation (PDF 136-170, printed 125-159) — annual
and quadrennial cycles, long-term athlete development, sensitive periods, talent
identification. Directly relevant to Baylor's multi-year athlete development question._

_Batch 4 (lowest priority for football): Chapter 5, Altitude training (PDF 171-212, printed
160-201). Recommend framework-only treatment (5-15 entries, confidence capped at `untested`)
or skipping entirely unless Eric names a specific altitude-camp use case — Baylor football
does not train at altitude as a standard practice per anything in `method-baseline.md`._

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): concurrent workloads compete for limited energy supply, differing
physiological-system restoration times leave athletes under-recovered for all targets at
once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits, technical complexity, neuromuscular
fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across many targets, and the training
stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be reached when it is divided
among many abilities.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete — the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own compatibility rule,
"you can't ride two horses with one saddle" — incompatible qualities are not both trained at
full intensity in the same block (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level — the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by this library's own Bompa & Haff 5th-edition material
(`periodization--bompa`), which is a current (not 1984-vintage) textbook still teaching and
defending a form of the traditional/complex periodization model for high-level athletes.
Issurin's critique in this chapter names Bompa's *1984* edition specifically (PDF p. 13,
printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the traditional model he is arguing
against — it is not a critique of the Bompa & Haff 5th edition already in this library,
which incorporates concentrated-loading and conjugated-sequence ideas closer to Issurin's
own. **Inference:** Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (2016, *Sports Medicine*,
"Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches," Zotero item
`PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached in this ingest) is titled around limitations as well as
benefits and likely narrows this 2008 book's confident framing; treat the frontmatter
`confidence: contested` as applying specifically to the universal "traditional doesn't work
for high performers" claim, not to the narrower, self-limited concentration principle.

**Example** — A collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.

**Related** — [[framework--block-periodization-mesocycle-taxonomy]] — the three-block
structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]] — converging concentrated-load
ideas already in this library. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (staging) —
check for overlap on why generalized simultaneous training under-delivers for advanced
athletes.

# Accumulation, Transmutation (Transformation), and Realization: the Three Mesocycle-Blocks

**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
(Table 1.7, PDF p. 37, printed p. 26): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration — fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,
event-specific tactics) at low-medium volume/high intensity, with full restoration required
going in. Each type has its own monitoring focus: basic-ability tests for accumulation,
sport-specific-ability tests for transmutation, and maximum speed/strategy checks for
realization. **Locator note:** the 1985 origin paper (Issurin & Kaverin) and this book's
1.2.1 narrative (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22) use the term **transformation**; from section
1.2.2 onward (PDF p. 37+, printed p. 26+) and in the book's own tables, the term used is
**transmutation**. Both names refer to the same middle block; record both because a search
for either term should resolve to this entry.

**Why it works** — The sequencing is designed to exploit the fact that different motor
abilities have different **residual training effect** durations (see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]): basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, max strength) decay slowest, so they can be built early and coast on their own
residual while transmutation and realization narrow the focus toward faster-decaying,
more specific and speed-dependent qualities close to competition. Issurin frames this as
superimposition of residual effects (Figure 1.8, PDF p. 39, printed p. 28) rather than
concurrent development of everything at once.

**When to apply** — Structuring a training stage (the accumulation-transmutation-realization
sequence, ending in competition) for advanced athletes who need multiple qualities peaked
together — see [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]] for how these three
blocks compose into a full annual plan. **Eric's baseline** shows a structurally similar but
independently-arrived-at sequence: the department's own preparatory-period design goes
hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md pp.43-48) —
a general-to-specific progression that parallels accumulation-to-realization, though the
baseline's sequence is not explicitly framed with Issurin's residual-effect superimposition
logic or his restoration-status distinctions between blocks.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a three-way classification built for advanced
athletes who can tolerate the fatigue-accumulating transmutation block (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] for the low-/mid-level-athlete
carve-out). It presumes a training stage that ends in a real competition or test date to
absorb the realization block's tapering logic; without a fixed target date, there is no
clear trigger for when accumulation should end and transmutation begin. **Contested (partly):**
the vault's Bompa & Haff material (`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`)
independently describes a comparable saturated-load-then-restitution structure with a

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. The stated physiological basis: aerobic endurance's
long residual rests on morphological/biochemical changes (aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
capillaries, hemoglobin, glycogen storage) that increase 40-90% with training; maximum
strength's residual rests on comparably substantial morphological, biochemical and neural
changes (fiber cross-section, hyperplasia, motor-unit recruitment/synchronization,
motor-neuron discharge frequency, citing Zatsiorsky, 1995); maximum speed's short residual
reflects much smaller adaptations (phosphocreatine +2-5%, peak lactate +10-20%, anaerobic
enzymes +2-20%, citing Thorstensson, 1988) riding on delicate, unstable neuromuscular
patterns that decay quickly without continued training.

**Why it works — Inference** — Larger, more structural adaptations (aerobic
enzymatic/capillary changes, strength's neural and hypertrophic changes) persist longer
because the underlying tissue/enzyme changes take longer to reverse than the smaller,
more neurally-dependent changes behind peak speed. The author does not present this as an
experimentally isolated causal mechanism within this book — it is a physiological
rationale offered alongside the cited numbers, not derived from a controlled decay study
run on the same subjects who produced the durations.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27) — this 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures closely enough that it is very likely
this table (or a source repeating it) is the origin of that course-material claim, though
neither source cites the other directly, so this should be confirmed with Eric rather than
asserted as fact.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. **Contested — flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same
baseline corpus states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "The traits easiest to
build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build
(alactic/speed) are lost slowest" (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47). This flatly contradicts both this table (aerobic residual
is the *longest*, tied with strength, at 30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest*
at 5±3 days) and the baseline's own class-1-transcript-sourced claim quoted above. Do not
harmonize these three data points — record all three with their locators and resolve with
Eric directly; this may reflect two different course sessions describing genuinely
different things (e.g., "detraining of an untrained quality" vs. "retention of a
peaked/tapered quality"), but that reconciliation is not stated anywhere in the corpus.
**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability — both describe
heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
as restating the same specific claim.

**Example** — In a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation (building
aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
realization, the aerobic and strength gains from accumulation are still within their ~30-day
residual window when realization begins, so they need no further direct stimulus — but if
maximum speed work is not re-introduced within about 5 days of the target competition, its
residual will have already decayed below peak by competition day.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts —
cross-reference, do not conflate),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

# The Training Stage (A-T-R + Competition) Is the Annual Plan's Building Block, Enabling Multiple Peaks

# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium

**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
athlete response. The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 Olympics — "the entire Olympic podium occupied by
athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).

**Why it works — the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** —
Issurin does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block
lengths (4/4/2 weeks) or this particular three-way split (by competitive readiness rather
than by ability type) were chosen; the mechanism offered is the same general BPC logic
(concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.

**When to apply — untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking (Bondarchuk predates and directly
inspired Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy, per PDF p. 32-33)
and as an alternative three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
(accumulation/transmutation/realization) — worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single coach's single-event outcome (n = 1
coaching program, one Olympic final) with no comparison group, no report of what other
finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and Issurin's own
secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy — see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
historically related, three-block system.

**Example** — A coach citing "block periodization has a track record" should specify
which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type blocks) and
should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one documented
historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]] — a comparable single-coach
case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault) — the *same* coach (Bondarchuk), but a completely different, unrelated framework
of his (an exercise-classification taxonomy by movement similarity, not a mesocycle-timing
system). The two should never be conflated when either is cited.

# World-Class Track and Field Athletes Compete and Peak Many Times Per Season, Not Once

**What it is** — Table 1.5 (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13, based on Suslov, 2001, with Issurin's
modifications) reports three world-class athletes' single-season competition patterns:
**Marion Jones** (100-200m, long jump; 1998 season) had **10 peaks** (8 in running, 2 in
long jump, all at personal-best level) across a **200-day** competitive span, with typical
19-22 day intervals between peaks. **Sergei Bubka** (pole vault; 1991 season) had **7
peaks** (all within 3% of his personal best, 595-612 cm) across a **265-day** span,
23-43 day intervals. **Stefka Kostadinova** (high jump; 1998 season) had **11 peaks** (all
within 3% of her personal best, 200-205 cm) across a combined **155-day** span (winter ~20
days; spring/summer 135 days), 14-25 day intervals. Issurin's summary point: these athletes'
5-8 month competitive spans "can not be subdivided into traditional preparatory and
competitive periods," yet their basic abilities (max strength, aerobic regeneration
capacity) still had to be maintained across that entire span.

**Why it works — this is observational, not interventional** — These are real competition
records for three specific, historically documented elite athletes (Olympic/World
champions), not an experiment; the "why" is a report of what elite competition calendars
actually looked like by 1991/1998, cited to Suslov's (2001) analysis rather than derived
from a controlled study of periodization models.

**When to apply** — As direct evidence for the strength-and-conditioning miss-log's
"peaking phase structure" gap: this table is the empirical case Issurin uses to argue that a
single annual peak (or even a two-/three-peak model) does not describe how modern elite
individual-sport athletes actually compete, which motivates the multi-stage annual model in
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]. Useful for framing the *problem*
(competition calendars now demand many peaks) to Baylor coaches even before the
*solution* (Chapter 3's microcycle-level guidance, not yet ingested) is available.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — All three examples are individual, non-contact,
technique/power sports (sprinting/jumping, pole vault, high jump) where "peak" can be defined
by a single measurable performance (time, height, distance) on a given day. **Inference:**
this evidence does not directly transfer to football, where "peak" is not a single
measurable output and the competitive calendar is fixed by a weekly game schedule rather
than a chosen sequence of meets — the multi-peak *problem* generalizes (a football season
also demands repeated high-level performance, not one), but the specific 19-43 day
inter-peak intervals shown here are specific to how often these particular athletes chose to
compete, not a transferable spacing rule for football practice or game weeks. Data source is
single (Suslov, 2001, "with modifications" by Issurin) with no stated method for how "peak"
was defined or verified for each performance.

**Example** — When explaining to a Baylor position group why in-season programming assumes
more than one readiness peak per season, this table is a citable, real-world existence proof
that elite athletes routinely peak 7-11 times in a season — useful for framing, not for
directly copying an inter-peak interval into a football in-season plan.

**Related** — [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]].

# Two Studies Issurin Cites Against Simultaneous Development: Swimmer Interference and Kayaker Decay

**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
concentrated blocks.

**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
improve; explosive strength *decreased* — despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation: extensive endurance
work captures the metabolic (anabolic) energy needed for the hypertrophy and neural-drive
adaptations that explosive/maximal strength require, and the resulting chronic fatigue keeps
central and peripheral neural factors from the state needed for strength gains
(citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point).

**(2) Kayaker decay under traditional periodization (PDF p. 25-26, printed pp. 14-15,
Figure 1.4 — the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic work and
maximum-strength work were reduced or dropped as "harmful for racing technique," and V-AT,
peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive period. Distance velocity
still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
reduced force — i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
was far from optimal."

**Why it works** — Both cases illustrate a different failure mode of the traditional,
simultaneous model: the swimmer case shows *concurrent* interference (training endurance and
strength together blunts the strength adaptation), while the kayaker case shows *sequential*
decay (abilities built early in the year are not maintained and fade by competition,
substituted for by other means). Both motivate Issurin's residual-effect-aware, consecutive
block sequencing (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]).

**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the stronger evidence of the two: it is a
controlled, measured 8-week study with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
letting it decay unaddressed."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
from this source alone — treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable without the
original 1986/whichever-year source Issurin drew Figure 1.3 from (not cited by name on this
page). **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
observational across one season with no control group — it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
the kayakers' single annual peak design.

**Example** — A Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
programmed.

**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (Table 1.4's rationale,
which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

# Key-Workouts and Key-Exercises Apply the Concentration Principle Inside a Single Session

**What it is** — Issurin extends the BPC concentration principle (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) down to the level of a single session.
A **key-workout** is the most important development session in a training cycle, focused on
the current main training emphasis (Table 2.5, PDF p. 56, printed p. 45): it targets the
cycle's most relevant abilities (usually one motor-fitness and one technique/tactics
target), demands focused athlete motivation and coach support, is timed for the athlete's
"best time" (adjusted to prior load but not overly fatigued), is loaded at a
substantial/large/extreme level, favors partnership/team-spirit organizational forms, and
requires thorough objective monitoring (chronometry, HR, blood lactate, video). New,
unfamiliar training means should *not* be introduced during a key-workout, since novelty
diverts attention and motivation from load-specific execution. Within a workout, the
analogous concept is the **key-exercise** (or **key-task** in team/combat sports where a
scrimmage or sparring session plays the role) — the single most important exercise, given
priority placement, maximal self-motivation and support, "prime-time" timing, and careful
monitoring (Table 2.9, PDF p. 64, printed p. 53). Issurin gives typical prescriptive ranges
for key-exercises by targeted ability (Table 2.10, PDF p. 67, printed p. 55, based on Fox &
Mathews 1981 and Viru 1995, "with author's modification"): maximal speed, 7-15s work at a
1:10 work/rest ratio, maximal intensity, 5-8 reps, 2-5 series; anaerobic glycolytic power,
30-50s, 1:(4-5), submaximal, 4-6 reps, 2-4 series, blood lactate >8 mmol/L and HR >180;
anaerobic glycolytic endurance, 1-1.5 min, 1:3, high intensity, 8-12 reps, 1-3 series,
maximal lactate >8 and HR >180; aerobic power, 1-2 min, 1:(1-0.5), intermediate, 5-8 reps,
1-3 series, lactate 4-8 and HR 160-180; aerobic endurance, 1-8 min, 1:0.3, medium intensity,
4-16 reps, 1-3 series, lactate 2.5-4(5) and HR 140-160; restoration/fat oxidation, 20-90 min,
low intensity, 1-3 reps, HR 100-140.

**Why it works** — Concentrating mental focus, coach attention, and objective load-tracking
on one workout and one exercise per cycle (rather than treating every session as equally
important) is the same logic as the chapter-1 concentration principle applied at a smaller
time scale: it protects a genuinely high-value stimulus from being diluted or blunted by
surrounding fatigue and divided attention.

**When to apply** — Programming a training cycle's hardest, most important session so it
actually gets the recovery state, attention, and monitoring it needs to produce the intended
adaptation, rather than treating every practice/lift as interchangeable. Table 2.10's
intervals give a concrete starting point for designing a key-exercise once the targeted
ability is chosen. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name an equivalent "key-workout"
concept explicitly, though the department's own metric-selection discipline (pick 1-2 output
metrics per force-plate report, per the Hawkin Dynamics ODSF framework,
`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring") reflects a similar
instinct toward concentrating monitoring attention rather than tracking everything equally.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own cautionary example (PDF p. 66, printed
p. 55) is that selecting the correct key-exercise is harder than it looks: at a national
coaching seminar of Olympic/World/Continental medalist-producing coaches, "more than 50%"
of proposed workouts confused exercises for maximal speed with exercises for speed endurance
(anaerobic glycolytic capacity), or aerobic endurance with aerobic power — i.e., experienced
coaches routinely mis-assign an exercise to the wrong physiological bucket. Table 2.10's
numeric ranges are themselves secondary citations (Fox & Mathews 1981; Viru 1995) filtered
through "author's modification" — the specific modification is not described, so treat the
exact numbers as Issurin's own adapted synthesis rather than a directly-reproduced published
table. This system also assumes a coach has the staff capacity for thorough, per-workout
objective monitoring (HR, blood lactate, video) — not always feasible outside individual/dual
sports with small rosters.

**Example** — For a football skill player whose training cycle emphasizes maximal speed,
the key-exercise might be 6-8 reps of 7-15s maximal-intensity sprints at roughly a 1:10
work-rest ratio (per Table 2.10), placed early in the week's most-rested session, with
sprint times or GPS max-velocity data as the monitored variable — while other exercises in
that same session are deliberately treated as secondary, not co-equal priorities.

[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]].

# Quantifying Workout Load on a 1-5 Scale, Mapped to Borg RPE Bands

**What it is** — Issurin presents a load-related workout classification built around three
functions: **development**, **retention**, and **restoration** (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41).
Table 2.3 (PDF p. 53, printed p. 42, based on Zatsiorsky 1995, modified by Issurin 2003)
quantifies this on a 1-5 scale using restoration time as the objective marker: restoration
level 1 (< 12 hours), retention level 2 (12-24 hours), development-substantial level 3
(24-48 hours), development-large level 4 (48-72 hours), development-extreme level 5
(> 72 hours). Because restoration-time-based classification does not fit every training type
well (Issurin notes coordination/neuro-emotional-stress workouts need less restoration time
than the scale implies), Table 2.4 (PDF p. 54, printed p. 43) offers a parallel mapping using
Borg's Rate of Perceived Exertion scale (Borg, 1973): RPE 6-11 (very-very-easy to
fairly-easy) = restoration; RPE 12-14 (slightly difficult) = retention; RPE 15-16
(difficult) = development-substantial; RPE 17-18 (very difficult) = development-large; RPE
19-20 (very-very difficult) = development-extreme.

**Why it works — inference on the underlying logic** — Restoration time and perceived
exertion are both proxies for how disruptive a session was to homeostasis; using either (or
both together) lets a coach assign every workout a comparable numeric load value even in
non-measurable sports (team sports, gymnastics), which Issurin identifies as the practical
payoff: "the load level of each workout can be quantified and expressed numerically" (PDF
p. 54, printed p. 43), enabling load-dependent categorization (development vs. retention vs.
restoration) across an entire training plan, not just isolated hard/easy labeling.

**When to apply** — Building a simple, athlete-reportable RPE-based load log for sports or
settings where objective physiological monitoring (HR, blood lactate) is not available for
every session; classifying a completed week of training after the fact into
development/retention/restoration proportions to check whether the intended block emphasis
(see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) was actually
delivered. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name Borg's RPE scale specifically, though
session-level subjective load tracking is philosophically consistent with the department's
general preference for practical, staff-sustainable monitoring tools over burdensome ones
(`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," on why daily wellness surveys were
abandoned when athletes learned to game them) — RPE has its own well-documented gaming risk
that is not addressed anywhere in this Issurin chapter and should be treated as an open
question, not assumed solved.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no mechanism** for why these
specific RPE cut-points (11/12, 14/15, 16/17, 18/19) map to these specific restoration-time
bands rather than some other set of cut-points; both tables are presented as ready-made
scales without a validation study cited in this chapter. RPE is a subjective, athlete-reported
measure and is vulnerable to the same reporting-fatigue and gaming dynamics documented
elsewhere for subjective wellness tools; do not treat it as equivalent in reliability to the
objective HR/blood-lactate markers used in Table 2.10's key-exercise prescriptions
(see [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]). The scale also does not
distinguish RPE driven by physical load from RPE driven by psychological/technical/cognitive
demand (e.g., a technically difficult but physically light session), a limitation Issurin
himself flags when noting coordination-heavy sessions need less restoration than their
subjective difficulty might imply.

**Example** — A coach without force-plate or HR-monitor access for every practice can have
players self-report session RPE, multiply by session duration (an approach not itself stated
in this chapter but a standard extension of Borg RPE elsewhere in sport science, noted here
as an inference, not something Issurin describes), and classify the week's development
vs. retention vs. restoration balance against the intended training-stage emphasis.

**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].
